claims.text: A hybrid machine-learning model trained on ab initio data for defective structures will predict the electrical conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than analytical models based on perfect crystals.
The modeled structures include both intrinsic defects and oxygen-induced defects.
The target samples are bulk HfNbTaTiZr with realistic intrinsic defect densities, including nominally pure and 1 wt.% oxygen-containing specimens.
The proposed regression framework uses descriptors derived from ab initio simulations of defective structures and oxygen configurations.
Quantum and impurity scattering effects dominate electrical transport between approximately 0 and 200 K.
Anharmonic phonon scattering is more significant between 300 and 1200 K.
Defect concentration and defect type, including oxygen-induced lattice distortions, modify carrier-scattering mechanisms and mobility.
Including lattice defects in the descriptors allows the model to represent additional scattering channels.
Lattice defects and oxygen impurities alter the alloy's band structure.
Defect-related scattering and band-structure changes produce temperature-dependent carrier mobilities different from those of a pristine crystal.
The hybrid model will follow experimental conductivity trends more closely in both specified temperature regimes.
The specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen will have lower conductivity than the nominally pure specimen.
The hybrid model will have lower prediction error than conventional analytical approaches.
Conventional approaches underestimate defect-induced scattering at low temperatures.
Conventional approaches inadequately represent high-temperature anharmonic effects.
Existing analytical predictions assume perfect, defect-free crystals and show significant discrepancies for HfNbTaTiZr containing realistic defects or oxygen.
The proposed applicability range is bulk HfNbTaTiZr with near-equilibrium defect levels, no more than 1 wt.% oxygen, and temperatures of 0–200 K or 300–1200 K.
Predictions for oxygen concentrations above 1 wt.% or highly non-equilibrium defect structures may require additional calibration.
The hypothesis is falsified if the hybrid model does not produce a statistically significant reduction in conductivity-prediction error relative to conventional analytical methods.
The hypothesis is also falsified if the model fails to predict the distinct conductivity deviation of the 1 wt.% oxygen specimen.
